slides.page_title: Lost Updates & Write Skew: The Anomalies That Bite (cont.)

items: Weakest to strongest, top to bottom.
`FOR UPDATE` never blocks a plain SELECT.
KEY SHARE is why child inserts no longer block parent updates.
Locks live in `xmax` + multixacts, held until COMMIT.
Never released early, not even after the statement.
`NOWAIT` raises 'could not obtain lock on row' at once.
Good for interactive UIs: fail, do not queue.
`SKIP LOCKED` skips rows another txn holds.
That is the standard way to build a work queue.

slides.page_title: Explicit Locks: Rows, Tables, and When to Reach for Them

blocks.title: How Migrations Kill Sites
blocks.text: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE conflicts with everything. An ALTER waiting on it queues every later query behind the request, and the site is down while nothing is even running.

lines: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
-- blocked ALTER fails fast, no queue

blocks.title: Guardrails
items: `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`: kills the abandoned txn holding everything hostage.
A holds row 1 and wants row 2.
B holds row 2 and wants row 1.

caption.text: Part 3 of POSTGRES TXN & LOCKING. Your Postgres default silently allows lost updates and write skew, and it never tells you. This 10-page field handbook walks the whole stack: MVCC internals and xmin/xmax, what each of the three real isolation levels still permits, row locks and SKIP LOCKED queues, deadlock causes with their fixes, and advisory locks for the things that aren't rows. Ends with a decision tree, a retry contract, and the monitoring queries to prove you got it right.
